t: Requirement-to-Test Mapper - Signature build-tool concept
title: Requirement-to-Test Mapper - Signature build-tool concept
definition: Connects each requirement to tests that verify it.
description:
Every build an AI undertakes passes through Requirement-to-Test Mapper: Connects each requirement to tests that verify it. The catalog lists it among the thousand fundamental build tools because no serious building happens without it. This database is its Signature edition - the concept rebuilt as a deterministic framework with seven pillars, grounded in real techniques and standards, and taught through a ladder of runnable drills.

The Signature line treats Requirement-to-Test Mapper as infrastructure, not inspiration. Infrastructure has contracts: given these inputs, in this state, the Requirement-to-Test Mapper produces that output, and anyone can verify it. The seven pillars are those contracts made concrete - each owns one responsibility, each can be tested alone, and together they compose into the full capability. The technique records show the real public knowledge the pillars stand on.

Work through this database the way you would commission a machine: read the charter in the overview, inspect each pillar, check the techniques against your own knowledge, then run the drills. Every record includes a program you can execute with node - the Requirement-to-Test Mapper is demonstrated, not merely described.

t: Signature Discoverer - Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework pillar
title: Signature Discoverer - Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework pillar
definition: The Discoverer component of the Signature Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework, owning discoverer. Signature concept.
description:
The Signature Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework decomposes the capability (Connects each requirement to tests that verify it.) into seven pillars, and the Discoverer is the one that owns the framework's discoverer responsibilities. Owning a responsibility means three things in the Signature line: the pillar declares exactly what it accepts, it publishes exactly what it guarantees, and it logs enough evidence that a third party can replay its work and reach the same conclusion.

This discipline pays off when builds go wrong, because they always eventually do. When a Requirement-to-Test Mapper result looks suspicious, the auditor does not re-run the whole build and hope; they replay the Discoverer's log, check its guarantees against its inputs, and find the fault at its source. The pillar is thus both a worker and a witness - it does the work and it testifies about the work.

Try it yourself: this record's demo runs the Discoverer's core procedure on a worked example. The program is plain JavaScript - save it as demo.js and run it with node, or press Run in the Demo Lab. Change the inputs and re-run; the procedure is deterministic, so you can verify every claim the description makes.

Signature framing: this pillar is part of the Signature line's original design for Requirement-to-Test Mapper. It is labeled a Signature concept throughout - an engineered proposal, not an established public fact. The techniques it relies on are real and cited in the technique records of this database.

t: Signature Validator - Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework pillar
title: Signature Validator - Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework pillar
definition: The Validator component of the Signature Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework, owning validator. Signature concept.
description:
The Validator is a load-bearing component of the Signature Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework. Its contract is narrow and absolute: within the framework, everything concerning the framework's validator responsibilities belongs to the Validator, and the Validator answers for it. This separation is what makes the framework testable - the Validator can be exercised alone, with declared inputs and checkable outputs, long before it is wired into a full build.

In operation the Validator works like this. A build request arrives carrying the Requirement-to-Test Mapper charter (connects each requirement to tests that verify it.). The Validator reads its portion of the charter, performs its transformation, and hands a verified intermediate result to the next pillar. If its checks fail, it stops the line and reports exactly what was wrong, instead of passing corruption downstream. That fail-fast discipline is the Signature line's signature.

Signature-concept illustration: a builder asks for an small universal job that needs Requirement-to-Test Mapper. The Validator takes the request's validator responsibilities slice, applies the framework's deterministic procedure, and returns its result with a proof of what it did. Run this record's demo program to see the Validator's core logic execute on a concrete example - the same logic, the same result, every run.

Signature framing: this pillar is part of the Signature line's original design for Requirement-to-Test Mapper. It is labeled a Signature concept throughout - an engineered proposal, not an established public fact. The techniques it relies on are real and cited in the technique records of this database.

definition: The Composer component of the Signature Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework, owning composer. Signature concept.
description:
Inside the Signature Requirement-to-Test Mapper framework, the Composer owns the framework's composer responsibilities. It accepts declared inputs, applies one deterministic transformation, and emits a result that any other pillar - or any auditor - can verify independently.

What distinguishes the Signature Composer from an ad-hoc script is the verification loop. Every execution is checked against the charter (Connects each requirement to tests that verify it.). If the result cannot be justified against the charter, it is rejected and the build halts with a diagnostic instead of a silent wrong answer. Deterministic builds are not a slogan here; they are the acceptance test.
